title: Git commands and their buttons
summary: status, add, commit, checkout, merge, push, pull and stash, each next to its Source Control button.

say.never: Every git command has a matching button or menu item in the **Source Control** panel on the left, and this lesson uses the buttons. The command names are listed here so you can recognise them in the team's docs and when other people talk about git. Same result either way.
say.bit: Every git command has a button or menu item in Source Control, and this lesson uses the buttons. The commands are here so you recognise the names.

say.never: `git status` asks: **what has changed?** It lists the files you've edited and tells you which branch you're on. **The button:** you don't need one, because the Source Control panel *is* the status. Edited files show up in the list under **Changes**, and a number appears on the icon.
say.bit: `git status` lists changed files and your branch. In Source Control the **Changes** list is the same information.

say.never: `git add` **stages** a file, which means "put it in the next save point". Typing it looks like the board. **The button:** hover over a file in the **Changes** list and click the **+**.
say.bit: `git add` stages a file for the next commit. **Button:** hover a file under Changes and press **+**.

say.never: `git commit` **saves the snapshot** of everything you staged, with a message. The `-m` means "here comes my message". **The button:** type your message in the box at the top of Source Control and press the blue **Commit** button.
say.bit: `git commit -m` saves the staged snapshot with a message. **Button:** write the message in the box and press **Commit**.

say.never: `git checkout` **moves you to another branch**. Add `-b` to make a new one first. **The button:** click the **branch name** in the bottom-left corner of the window. A menu opens where you can pick a branch or choose **Create new branch**.
say.bit: `git checkout` switches branch (`-b` creates it). **Button:** the branch name in the bottom-left corner opens the branch menu.

board.code:
git checkout develop
git checkout -b issue-30-add-intake-sensor

say.never: `git merge` **brings another branch's work into the one you're on**. First move to the branch that should receive the work. **The button:** in Source Control, click the **...** (more actions) menu, then **Branch**, then **Merge...**, and pick the branch to bring in.
say.bit: `git merge` brings another branch's commits into your current branch. **Button:** Source Control **...** menu, then Branch, then Merge.

board.code:
git checkout develop
git merge issue-30-add-intake-sensor

marks.label: into the branch you are on

say.never: The **remote** is the shared copy of the project (on GitHub). `git push` **sends** your commits there so teammates can see them. `git pull` **fetches** their new commits and brings them into your branch. **The button:** in Source Control, click **...**, then **Pull, Push**, and choose **Pull**, **Push** or **Push to...**. (In this lesson the blue Publish Branch and Sync buttons are hidden, so use that menu.)
say.bit: `git push` uploads your commits to the remote (`origin`); `git pull` downloads and merges others'. **Button:** **...** menu, then Pull, Push (Pull, Push or Push to...).

board.code:
git push origin issue-30-add-intake-sensor
git pull

say.never: `git stash` puts your **unfinished** changes on a shelf and gives you a clean folder, so you can switch branches. `git stash pop` takes them back off the shelf. **The button:** in Source Control, click **...**, then **Stash**, then **Stash**. To get them back, **...**, **Stash**, **Pop Latest Stash**.
say.bit: `git stash` shelves uncommitted changes so you can switch branches; `git stash pop` restores them. **Button:** Source Control **...** menu, then Stash.

board.code:
git stash
git checkout develop
# ...fix something, commit...
git checkout issue-30-add-intake-sensor
git stash pop

say.never: When a feature is done, you **merge** it into `develop`. If two branches changed the *same line*, git doesn't know which to keep, so it stops and asks you. That's a **merge conflict**. Don't panic: the exercises walk you through one. The commands and buttons above are everything you need for the whole lesson.
say.bit: Finished features merge into `develop`. Two branches changing the same line is a merge conflict, and git asks you to choose; the exercises cover it.
